title: Roughing a green birch kuksa blank
subtitle: Green-woodwork: axe and sloyd knife roughing before the hook knife
excerpt: The first stage of a kuksa: roughing the exterior from a green birch billet with a carving axe and sloyd knife before the hook knife work begins. Getting the blank to the right thickness and profile before hollowing is the step most beginners skip, and the step that determines whether the finished kuksa is well-balanced or clumsy.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the kuksa blank method; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the axe-to-knife progression on round-form billets.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. The axe removes large amounts of green birch quickly and the sloyd knife shapes it with minimal resistance.
A Sámi-tradition single-piece carved drinking cup, traditionally made from birch burl. Here applied to a burl-free birch blank version.
A short length of split timber; here, a section of green birch for the kuksa.
The rough-shaped piece of wood from which the finished kuksa will be hollowed.

content.text: is a single-piece carved drinking cup with a deep hollow body and a long handle. Traditionally made from birch burl, a standard green birch
makes a serviceable kuksa without the difficulty of sourcing a burl. This pattern covers the roughing stage only: carving the exterior profile and bringing the
to the correct wall thickness before the hook knife begins. A well-roughed blank makes the hollow straight forward; a poorly roughed one makes it almost impossible to achieve even walls.
. Source a birch billet with a diameter of at least 8 cm for a small kuksa (holds about 250 ml). A 10, 12 cm diameter billet gives more working room.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.

One birch billet, 16 cm long, at least 8 cm diameter. Cut across the grain so the blank includes both the pith and the outer rings. The pith side will become the interior of the cup; the outer ring side will become the base. Birch is the traditional kuksa timber for its pale colour and food-safety. Sycamore is the direct British alternative.
A carving stool with a splitting block nearby for the axe roughing. The sloyd knife work can be done on the lap.

Draw the kuksa profile on the end-grain face: the cup body is a 6 cm wide oval with its flat base at the outer ring of the billet (away from the pith), rising in a gentle dome. The handle projects from one side, 8 cm long, 3 cm wide. Mark the handle axis on the side of the billet. The cup opening will be carved from the pith side.

Use the carving axe to shape the handle: first flat-chop the top and bottom faces of the handle to its 3 cm height; then shape the sides. The axe cuts should be long, with the grain, removing large chips. The handle needs to be finished to within 5 mm of final size with the axe before the sloyd knife takes over.

Shape the outside of the cup body to a smooth rounded form, working the axe along the grain from the base rim toward the open top. The base should be flat enough to sit without rocking. Bring the walls to about 15 mm at this stage. The sloyd knife will reduce them further, and the hook knife will reach the final 5, 7 mm.
Step 4: Refine with the sloyd knife

to smooth the cup exterior and refine the handle profile. Bring the cup walls to 12 mm thickness, measured regularly by pressing a thumbnail through the wood, in green birch you can feel the resistance change as the wall gets thin. Use
for the curved transition between handle and cup body. This is the section where grain changes direction, read the grain before each cut and adjust direction accordingly.
Step 5: Check and hand off to hollowing

The blank is ready for hook knife hollowing when: the exterior profile is smooth with no flat spots; the walls are even at 12 mm; the base is flat enough to stand; the handle is close to final form. Mark the opening on the top face, a 55 mm oval centred on the cup axis, before handing off to the hook knife work.

Once the blank is roughed, the hook knife hollowing work follows the same principle as a deep-bowl spoon but at larger scale: begin at the rim and work inward in concentric passes, checking wall thickness from the side with strong light behind. See the hook-knife technique guide for the full hollow sequence.
Larger kuksa: 12 cm diameter billet for a hold-about-400 ml cup.
Sycamore kuksa: same profile, sycamore dries paler than birch and stays food-safe.

attrs.symptom: The axe tears long strips from the cup exterior rather than cutting cleanly
attrs.cause: Cutting against the grain, the axe is hitting the wood from the base toward the open end, which goes uphill against the grain on this blank
attrs.fix: Reverse direction: cut from the open end toward the base. The grain in a round billet runs radially outward; cut with it (toward the outside surface) rather than across it.
